questions.question: What does 'IP' stand for in IP Law?
choices: International Policy
Intellectual Property
Internal Protocol
Institutional Practice
questions.explanation: IP stands for Intellectual Property — legal rights over creations of the mind.

questions.question: How long does a standard patent last from the date of filing?
choices: 10 years
15 years
20 years
Life of the inventor plus 50 years
questions.explanation: Patents generally last 20 years from the filing date, subject to maintenance fees.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a requirement for patentability?
choices: Novelty
Inventive step
Industrial application
Aesthetic beauty
questions.explanation: The three requirements are novelty, inventive step (non-obviousness), and industrial applicability. Aesthetics is irrelevant.

questions.question: What does copyright protect?
choices: Ideas and concepts
Original works of authorship fixed in a tangible medium
Business methods
Domain names
questions.explanation: Copyright protects original expression fixed in a tangible medium, not ideas themselves.

questions.question: What is a trademark?
choices: A patent on a brand name
A sign that distinguishes goods or services of one trader from another
A license to sell goods
A registered business name
questions.explanation: A trademark is any sign capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of others.

questions.question: What is the general term of copyright protection in the EU?
choices: 25 years after publication
50 years after creation
Life of the author plus 70 years
100 years from creation
questions.explanation: In the EU, copyright lasts for the life of the author plus 70 years.

questions.question: What does 'prior art' mean in patent law?
choices: Art created before the Renaissance
All publicly available information before the patent filing date
Previous patents by the same inventor
Artwork related to the invention
questions.explanation: Prior art encompasses all publicly available information before the filing date that may be relevant to novelty and inventive step.

questions.question: Can a trademark be renewed indefinitely?
choices: No, trademarks expire after 25 years
Yes, as long as renewal fees are paid and it remains in use
Only if the owner is the original registrant
Only once
questions.explanation: Trademarks can be renewed indefinitely in 10-year periods, provided fees are paid and the mark remains in use.

questions.question: What is a 'trade secret'?
choices: A patented formula
Confidential business information that provides a competitive advantage
A type of trademark
A government classification
questions.explanation: Trade secrets are confidential information with commercial value that the holder takes reasonable steps to keep secret.

questions.question: Which international agreement establishes minimum IP protection standards for WTO members?
choices: The Berne Convention
The Paris Convention
TRIPS Agreement
The Hague Convention
questions.explanation: TRIPS (Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights) sets minimum IP standards for all WTO members.

questions.question: Does copyright require registration to exist?
choices: Yes, always
No, it arises automatically upon creation
Only for literary works
Only in common law countries
questions.explanation: Copyright arises automatically when an original work is fixed in a tangible medium. Registration is optional but can provide benefits.

questions.question: What is 'fair use' (or 'fair dealing')?
choices: Using a trademark without permission
A defense allowing limited use of copyrighted material without permission
Sharing patents for free
Trading IP rights on the open market
questions.explanation: Fair use/fair dealing is a legal doctrine permitting limited use of copyrighted works for purposes like criticism, education, or parody.

questions.question: What is a 'design right'?
choices: The right to design buildings
Protection for the visual appearance of a product
A patent for software
A right to modify someone else's work
questions.explanation: Design rights protect the appearance (shape, pattern, ornamentation) of a product, not its function.

questions.question: What is the 'Paris Convention'?
choices: An agreement on climate change
An international treaty on industrial property (patents, trademarks)
A convention on human rights
A trade agreement between France and the UK
questions.explanation: The Paris Convention (1883) is a foundational treaty on industrial property, establishing priority rights and national treatment.

questions.question: What are 'moral rights' in copyright law?
choices: The right to earn money from a work
Personal rights of the author, including attribution and integrity
Rights based on ethical standards
The right to censor offensive content
questions.explanation: Moral rights include the right of attribution (paternity) and the right to object to derogatory treatment of the work (integrity).

questions.question: What is a 'patent claim'?
choices: A lawsuit for patent infringement
The part of a patent that legally defines the scope of protection
A request for a patent extension
An objection to a patent application
questions.explanation: Patent claims define the boundaries of the patent protection — what is and is not covered by the patent.

questions.question: What is the 'priority right' under the Paris Convention?
choices: The right to be the first to use a trademark
The right to claim the filing date of an earlier application in another country
The right to priority processing by the patent office
The right to prevent others from filing similar patents
questions.explanation: Priority right allows an applicant to use the filing date of a first application in one country when filing in another within 12 months (patents) or 6 months (trademarks).

questions.question: What is 'patent infringement'?
choices: Filing a patent application
Making, using, or selling a patented invention without the patent holder's permission
Failing to pay patent fees
Publishing a patent specification
questions.explanation: Patent infringement occurs when someone makes, uses, sells, or imports a patented invention without authorization.

questions.question: What is the 'doctrine of equivalents' in patent law?
choices: All patents have equal value
Infringement can occur even if the infringing product is not identical but performs substantially the same function
Two patents covering the same invention are equivalent
Patent fees must be equivalent across countries
questions.explanation: The doctrine of equivalents allows a patent holder to claim infringement even when the accused product doesn't literally fall within the claims but is substantially similar.

questions.question: What is 'trademark dilution'?
choices: Mixing trademark chemicals
Weakening of a famous mark's distinctiveness through unauthorized use
Reducing the number of trademark classes
Sharing trademark rights among partners
questions.explanation: Trademark dilution occurs when use of a similar mark weakens the distinctiveness or tarnishes the reputation of a famous mark.

questions.question: What does the PCT (Patent Cooperation Treaty) facilitate?
choices: Automatic worldwide patent protection
A unified international filing procedure for seeking patent protection in multiple countries
Free licensing of patents
Standardized patent fees globally
questions.explanation: The PCT provides a single international filing procedure but does NOT grant an international patent — national/regional examination is still required.

questions.question: What is 'exhaustion of rights' (first sale doctrine) in IP law?
choices: When an IP right expires
After the first authorized sale, the IP holder cannot control further distribution of that specific item
When an inventor runs out of ideas
When a trademark becomes generic
questions.explanation: Exhaustion means that once an IP-protected product is sold with the rights holder's consent, they cannot restrict its further resale.

questions.question: What is a 'compulsory license' in patent law?
choices: A license that must be purchased before using any technology
A government-authorized license allowing use of a patent without the holder's consent
A mandatory training certificate for patent attorneys
A license required to file patent applications
questions.explanation: Compulsory licenses allow governments to authorize production of a patented product without the patent holder's consent, typically for public health reasons.

questions.question: What is 'secondary meaning' in trademark law?
choices: A trademark's literal translation
When a descriptive term acquires distinctiveness through use
The hidden meaning of a brand name
A trademark used for a secondary product line
questions.explanation: Secondary meaning (acquired distinctiveness) occurs when consumers associate a descriptive term with a specific source through extensive use.

questions.question: What is the 'Berne Convention'?
choices: A patent treaty
An international copyright treaty ensuring mutual recognition of copyright between member states
A trade secret protection agreement
A trademark harmonization treaty
questions.explanation: The Berne Convention (1886) is the principal international copyright treaty, establishing principles like automatic protection and national treatment.

questions.question: What is a 'cease and desist' letter in IP enforcement?
choices: A court order to stop infringing activity
A formal letter demanding that the recipient stop alleged infringing activity
A patent application withdrawal
A trademark cancellation request
questions.explanation: A cease and desist letter is a pre-litigation step where the IP holder formally demands the alleged infringer stop the infringing activity.

questions.question: Can software be patented?
choices: Never, under any circumstances
Yes, if it produces a technical effect beyond normal computer interaction
Only in the United States
Only if it includes hardware components
questions.explanation: In many jurisdictions, software-implemented inventions can be patented if they produce a further technical effect, though pure software 'as such' may be excluded.

questions.question: What is 'trademark genericide'?
choices: When a trademark is used for generic goods
When a trademark becomes the common name for a product and loses protection
When a generic product copies a trademark
When a trademark is translated to another language
questions.explanation: Genericide occurs when a trademark becomes so commonly used as a generic term (e.g., 'aspirin', 'escalator') that it loses its distinctiveness and protection.

questions.question: What is an 'injunction' in IP litigation?
choices: A monetary award
A court order requiring a party to do or refrain from doing something
A patent claim amendment
A licensing agreement
questions.explanation: An injunction is a court order that can prohibit ongoing infringement (prohibitory) or compel specific action (mandatory).

questions.question: What does WIPO stand for?
choices: World Intellectual Property Organization
World International Patent Office
Western Industrial Property Office
World Innovation and Progress Organization
questions.explanation: WIPO (World Intellectual Property Organization) is a UN agency that administers international IP treaties and promotes IP protection globally.

questions.question: What is the 'inventive step' (non-obviousness) requirement for patents?
choices: The invention must be completely new
The invention must not be obvious to a person skilled in the art
The invention must be commercially viable
The invention must be superior to existing products
questions.explanation: Inventive step requires that the invention would not have been obvious to a person with ordinary skill in the relevant field, considering the prior art.

questions.question: In EU trademark law, what is the 'likelihood of confusion' test?
choices: Whether consumers are confused about IP law
Whether the average consumer might believe goods/services come from the same or related source
Whether two trademarks look identical
Whether a product is confusingly designed
questions.explanation: Likelihood of confusion assesses whether the average consumer, considering all circumstances, might believe the goods/services originate from the same undertaking.

questions.question: What is the 'three-step test' in copyright law?
choices: A test for originality
A framework for permissible exceptions: special cases, no conflict with normal exploitation, no unreasonable prejudice
A filing procedure for copyright
A test for determining authorship
questions.explanation: The three-step test (Berne Convention Art. 9(2), TRIPS Art. 13) limits copyright exceptions to: (1) special cases, (2) not conflicting with normal exploitation, (3) not unreasonably prejudicing the author's interests.

questions.question: What is 'claim construction' in patent litigation?
choices: Building a patent application
The judicial interpretation of the meaning and scope of patent claims
Drafting new patent claims
Constructing prior art arguments
questions.explanation: Claim construction is the process by which a court interprets the terms and scope of patent claims to determine what is protected.

questions.question: What is a 'Supplementary Protection Certificate' (SPC)?
choices: An additional patent for improvements
An extension of patent protection for pharmaceutical/plant protection products to compensate for regulatory approval delays
A certificate of authenticity
A supplementary trademark registration
questions.explanation: SPCs extend patent protection for up to 5 years for medicinal/plant protection products to compensate for the time spent obtaining regulatory approval.

questions.question: What is 'contributory infringement' in patent law?
choices: Directly infringing a patent
Supplying a component or material that is especially suited for use in a patented invention
Filing a competing patent
Failing to cite prior art
questions.explanation: Contributory infringement occurs when a party supplies a component with no substantial non-infringing use, knowing it will be used to infringe a patent.

questions.question: What is the 'database right' in EU law?
choices: Copyright in software databases
A sui generis right protecting the investment in obtaining, verifying, or presenting database contents
A right to access government databases
A patent on database technology
questions.explanation: The EU Database Directive creates a sui generis right protecting substantial investment in obtaining, verifying, or presenting database contents, separate from copyright.

questions.question: What is 'patent trolling'?
choices: Searching for patents online
An entity acquiring patents primarily to extract licensing fees through litigation rather than using the patented technology
Filing multiple patent applications
Criticizing the patent system
questions.explanation: Patent trolls (non-practicing entities) acquire patents not to produce goods but to generate revenue through licensing demands and infringement lawsuits.

questions.question: What is 'FRAND' licensing?
choices: Free and non-discriminatory licensing
Fair, Reasonable, and Non-Discriminatory licensing terms for standard-essential patents
Franchise and distribution licensing
Federal registration and national disclosure
questions.explanation: FRAND (Fair, Reasonable, and Non-Discriminatory) terms are commitments made by holders of standard-essential patents to license on equitable terms.

questions.question: What is the 'originality' threshold for copyright protection in EU law after the Infopaq decision?
choices: The work must be commercially successful
The work must be the author's own intellectual creation
The work must be registered with a national office
The work must demonstrate artistic merit
questions.explanation: The CJEU in Infopaq (C-5/08) established that copyright subsists when a work is the 'author's own intellectual creation,' harmonizing the originality standard across the EU.

questions.question: What is 'patent prosecution'?
choices: Criminal proceedings for patent fraud
The process of negotiating with a patent office to obtain a patent grant
Suing someone for patent infringement
Cancelling an existing patent
questions.explanation: Patent prosecution is the interaction between an applicant and the patent office during examination, responding to objections and amending claims to secure a grant.

questions.question: What is the principle of 'national treatment' in IP treaties?
choices: Each country can set its own IP laws without restriction
Foreign nationals must receive the same IP protection as domestic nationals
IP rights only apply within the granting nation
National governments control all IP licensing
questions.explanation: National treatment (a cornerstone of the Paris and Berne Conventions) requires member states to grant foreign nationals the same IP protection as their own citizens.

questions.question: What is 'patent claim dependency'?
choices: A patent that relies on another patent
A dependent claim that refers back to and further limits an independent claim
When a company is dependent on its patent portfolio
The relationship between filing and examination
questions.explanation: A dependent claim incorporates all limitations of the claim it depends on and adds further narrowing features, creating a hierarchy of protection.

questions.question: What are 'orphan works' in copyright law?
choices: Works created by minors
Works whose copyright holder cannot be identified or located despite diligent search
Works in the public domain
Unpublished manuscripts
questions.explanation: Orphan works are copyrighted works whose rights holders cannot be found, creating challenges for digitization and reuse projects.

questions.question: What is the 'unitary patent' system in Europe?
choices: A single patent valid in all EU member states without individual validation
A patent that can only cover one invention
The standard European Patent Office procedure
A patent valid only in one country
questions.explanation: The Unitary Patent (effective 2023) provides patent protection across participating EU member states through a single registration, reducing costs and complexity.

cases.title: FreshBrew v. MermaidBeans
cases.context: FreshBrew Coffee Ltd. has operated a chain of coffee shops since 2015 under a registered trademark featuring a green mermaid logo. In early 2024, a new competitor called MermaidBeans opened several locations using a nearly identical green mermaid logo with only minor stylistic differences. FreshBrew has filed suit alleging trademark infringement.

questions.question: What type of intellectual property right is primarily at issue in this dispute?
choices: Patent right
Trademark right
Copyright
Trade secret
questions.explanation: The dispute centers on a registered trademark — a distinctive sign (the green mermaid logo) used to identify the source of goods and services.

questions.question: Which factor is MOST important in assessing whether MermaidBeans infringes FreshBrew's trademark?
choices: Whether MermaidBeans sells the same type of coffee beans
Whether there is a likelihood of confusion among average consumers
Whether MermaidBeans registered their logo first
Whether FreshBrew's logo is aesthetically superior
questions.explanation: Likelihood of confusion is the central test in trademark infringement — whether consumers might believe the goods come from the same or a related source.

questions.question: What is the first legal remedy FreshBrew should seek to stop MermaidBeans from using the logo immediately?
choices: Criminal prosecution
An interim injunction (preliminary injunction)
Filing a new patent application
Requesting arbitration
questions.explanation: An interim injunction can quickly prohibit the infringing use while the full case proceeds, preventing ongoing harm to the brand.

questions.question: From whose perspective is the likelihood of confusion assessed?
choices: The trademark examiner
The average consumer of the relevant goods or services
The trademark owner's legal team
An IP law professor
questions.explanation: Likelihood of confusion is assessed from the perspective of the average consumer who is reasonably well-informed and reasonably observant.

cases.title: NovaPharma v. GeneriCure
cases.context: NovaPharma holds a patent for a novel cancer drug delivery mechanism using lipid nanoparticles. The patent was granted in 2018 and contains claims covering the specific particle size range and coating method. GeneriCure has developed a similar drug using a slightly different molecular arrangement but achieving the same therapeutic effect through a substantially similar mechanism.

questions.question: What is the first step a court must take to determine whether GeneriCure's drug infringes the patent?
choices: Compare the prices of both drugs
Perform claim construction to interpret the scope of NovaPharma's patent claims
Ask NovaPharma's scientists for their opinion
Check whether GeneriCure filed any patents of its own
questions.explanation: Claim construction — the judicial interpretation of patent claim terms and scope — must precede any infringement analysis.

questions.question: Even though GeneriCure uses a 'slightly different molecular arrangement,' NovaPharma might still prevail under which legal doctrine?
choices: Fair use doctrine
Doctrine of equivalents
Exhaustion of rights
First-to-file principle
questions.explanation: The doctrine of equivalents extends patent protection to products that perform substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result.

questions.question: GeneriCure argues it began testing its drug solely to prepare a regulatory submission. Which exemption might protect this activity?
choices: Fair use defense
The Bolar exemption (regulatory use exemption)
Compulsory license
Prior user right
questions.explanation: The Bolar exemption allows generic manufacturers to conduct experiments and tests necessary for regulatory approval before a patent expires, without constituting infringement.

questions.question: If NovaPharma wins, how are damages typically calculated in pharmaceutical patent cases?
choices: Fixed statutory amount per pill sold
Lost profits or a reasonable royalty based on the infringer's sales
The total R&D cost of the original drug
A percentage of the infringer's total company revenue
questions.explanation: Damages are typically calculated as the patent holder's lost profits or, alternatively, a reasonable royalty that would have been agreed in a hypothetical negotiation.

cases.title: The Digital Canvas Dispute
cases.context: Digital artist Elara Voss used an AI image generation tool to create a series of surrealist artworks, which she then refined with manual editing. She registered copyright in the works and licensed them to a gallery for commercial prints. Photographer Marcus Chen later discovered that several of his copyrighted photographs were part of the AI tool's training dataset, and elements of his distinctive style appear in Elara's AI-generated pieces.

questions.question: What is the central question regarding copyright in Elara's AI-generated artworks?
choices: Whether digital art can ever be copyrighted
Whether there is sufficient human authorship and creative control to qualify for copyright protection
Whether the AI tool company owns all generated images
Whether Elara paid the correct licensing fee
questions.explanation: Copyright requires human authorship. The key question is whether Elara exercised sufficient creative choices (prompts, selection, editing) to constitute authorship, or whether the output is primarily machine-generated.

questions.question: If Marcus claims Elara's works are unauthorized derivatives of his photographs, what must he prove?
choices: That his photos are more aesthetically pleasing
That Elara's works incorporate substantial protectable expression from his photographs
That any AI-generated image using training data is automatically infringing
That he filed his copyright registration before Elara
questions.explanation: For a derivative work claim, Marcus must show that protectable expression — not just style or ideas — from his photographs was copied and incorporated into the new works.

questions.question: What rights does Marcus have regarding the use of his photographs in the AI's training dataset?
choices: None, because posting photos online grants universal permission
Potentially a reproduction right claim, unless a text and data mining exception applies
He can only claim rights if he registered a patent on his photos
His only option is to sue the AI company for defamation
questions.explanation: Feeding copyrighted works into training datasets involves reproduction. Marcus may have a claim unless a statutory exception (such as the EU's text and data mining exception) applies.

questions.question: The AI tool company argues that training on copyrighted images is permissible. Under EU law, which provision is most relevant to this defense?
choices: The right of parody under the Copyright Directive
The text and data mining (TDM) exceptions in Articles 3 and 4 of the DSM Directive
The database right under the Database Directive
The safe harbor provision for internet service providers
questions.explanation: Articles 3 and 4 of the EU Digital Single Market Directive provide TDM exceptions — Article 3 for research organizations and Article 4 for commercial TDM (unless rights holders have opted out).
